questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the exact solutions to the equation $\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-{90}^{∘})=-1$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x-{90}^{∘} & =-{45}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving our equation for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={90}^{∘}-{45}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘} \\ x & ={45}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘}.$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x={45}^{∘}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x={225}^{∘}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘}.$ So, the solutions are $x={45}^{∘},{225}^{∘}.$

Finally, the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ is $45\cdot 225=10\,125.$

questions.problem: Consider the equation $\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x+\frac{7\pi }{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ for $0\le x<2\pi .$ If the exact solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}$ are written in ascending order, what is the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\frac{7\pi }{3} & =\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =-\frac{7\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ 2x & =-\frac{13\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ x & =-\frac{13\pi }{12}+\frac{n\pi }{2} \\ x & =\frac{(6n-13)\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$

- Setting $n=3$ gives $x=\frac{5\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=4$ gives $x=\frac{11\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=5$ gives $x=\frac{17\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=6$ gives $x=\frac{23\pi }{12}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x=\frac{5\pi }{12},\,\frac{11\pi }{12},\,\frac{17\pi }{12},\,\frac{23\pi }{12}.
$$

Finally, since ${x}_{1}=\frac{5\pi }{12}$ and ${x}_{4}=\frac{23\pi }{12},$ we have

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{4}=\frac{5\pi }{12}+\frac{23\pi }{12}=\frac{28\pi }{12}=\frac{7\pi }{3}.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the equation $\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\sqrt{3}=0$ for $0\le x<2\pi .$ If the exact solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}$ are written in ascending order, what is the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\sqrt{3} & =0 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-\frac{\pi }{2} & =-\frac{\pi }{3}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{3}+n\pi  \\ 2x & =\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{12}+\frac{n\pi }{2} \\ x & =\frac{(1+6n)\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=\frac{\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{7\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x=\frac{13\pi }{12}$

- Setting $n=3$ gives $x=\frac{19\pi }{12}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{12},\frac{7\pi }{12},\frac{13\pi }{12},\frac{19\pi }{12}.
$$

Finally, since ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{12}$ and ${x}_{4}=\frac{19\pi }{12},$ we have

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{4}=\frac{\pi }{12}+\frac{19\pi }{12}=\frac{20\pi }{12}=\frac{5\pi }{3}.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the equation $\sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6})+3=0$ for $-\pi <x\le \pi .$ If the exact solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}$ are written in ascending order, what is the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6})+3 & =0 \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6}) & =-3 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6}) & =-\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6}) & =-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\frac{\pi }{6} & =-\frac{\pi }{3}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =-\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ 2x & =-\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi  \\ x & =-\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{n\pi }{2} \\ x & =\frac{(2n-1)\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\pi <x\le \pi .$

- Setting $n=-1$ gives $x=-\frac{3\pi }{4}$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=-\frac{\pi }{4}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x=\frac{3\pi }{4}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\pi <x\le \pi .$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x=-\frac{3\pi }{4},\,-\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{3\pi }{4}
$$

Finally, since ${x}_{1}=-\frac{3\pi }{4}$ and ${x}_{4}=\frac{3\pi }{4},$ we have

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{4}=-\frac{3\pi }{4}+\frac{3\pi }{4}=0.
$$

questions.problem:
Expressed in **ascending order** in radians, the **exact solutions** to the equation  $\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x)=-1,$ for $-\pi \le x<\pi ,$  are

${x}_{1}=$
{{field-1}}$,\,{x}_{2}=$
{{field-2}}$,\,{x}_{3}=$
{{field-3}}$,\,{x}_{4}=$
{{field-4}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =-\frac{\pi }{4}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving our equation for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{n\pi }{2} \\ x & =\frac{(4n-1)\pi }{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\pi \le x<\pi .$

- Setting $n=-1$ gives $x=-\frac{5\pi }{8}$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=-\frac{\pi }{8}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{3\pi }{8}$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x=\frac{7\pi }{8}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\pi \le x<\pi .$ 

So, in ascending order,  the solutions are 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{5\pi }{8},\,{x}_{2}=-\frac{\pi }{8},\,{x}_{3}=\frac{3\pi }{8},\,{x}_{4}=\frac{7\pi }{8}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving a Trigonometric Equation Containing the Tangent Function Transformed by Multiple Operations
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{3})-2 & =0 \\ 2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{3}) & =2 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We will find the general solution to the equation and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\frac{\pi }{3} & =\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =-\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ 2x & =-\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ x & =-\frac{\pi }{12}+\frac{n\pi }{2} \\ x & =\frac{(6n-1)\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,\ldots$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0 \leq x \lt 2\pi.$ Notice that setting $n=0$ gives a result outside of the domain.

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{12}.$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x=\dfrac{11\pi}{12}.$

- Setting $n=3$ gives $x=\dfrac{17\pi}{12}.$

- Setting $n=4$ gives $x=\dfrac{23\pi}{12}.$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0 \leq x \lt 2\pi.$ So, the solutions $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}, \dfrac{11\pi}{12}, \dfrac{17\pi}{12}, \dfrac{23\pi}{12} .
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+\frac{\pi }{4} & =\frac{\pi }{4}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & =-\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{4}+n\pi  \\ 3x & =n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{n\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,\ldots,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\pi < x \leq \pi.$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=0.$

- Setting $n=\pm1$ gives $x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

- Setting $n=\pm2$ gives $x=\pm\dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$

- Setting $n=3$ gives $x=\pi.$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\pi < x \leq \pi.$ So, the solutions are

$$
x = 0,\, \pm \dfrac{\pi}{3},\, \pm\dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \, \pi.
$$
